title: Harun al-Rashid and the Three Poets

full_text:
One evening, the Caliph Harun al-Rashid sat in his imperial salon in Baghdad, surrounded by his vizier Ja'afar, his courtiers, and three famous poets: Abu Nowas, Abu al-Atahiyah, and Al-Raqqashi. The hall was fragrant with ambergris, and crystal lamps illuminated the marble fountains.

The Caliph turned to the poets and commanded: 'Let each of you recite four lines describing the true condition of kings, that we may see whose verse touches the core of reality.'

Al-Raqqashi stepped forward, bowed low, and recited verses of lavish flattery:
'The world is yours, O King, from dawn to setting sun,
Thy sword commands the stars, thy will is ever done;
The nations bow their heads, thy glory shall not fade,
Eternal as the hills thy golden throne is made!'

Harun al-Rashid listened with a faint, weary smile, having heard such flattery a thousand times.

Abu Nowas stepped forward next, reciting with his customary sparkling wit:
'Enjoy the fragrant feast, the music of the lute,
Before the turning sphere makes every dancer mute;
Gather the rose of joy while youth and fortune smile,
For life is but a dream that lasts a little while!'

The Caliph nodded, pleased by the poet's merry elegance.

Finally, the ascetic poet Abu al-Atahiyah stepped forward, his eyes burning with moral conviction. He declaimed in a ringing voice:
'Rejoice within thy palace walls, O King of mighty power,
Yet know that death shall knock upon thy portal at its hour;
When all thy guards are sleeping and thy breath begins to fail,
Thy gold and armies shall not weigh a feather on the scale;
Only the justice thou hast wrought, the tears thou hast relieved,
Shall stand as witness for thy soul before the throne received!'

The entire court fell into dead silence. Harun al-Rashid covered his face with his mantle and wept bitterly, moved by the solemn truth.

The Caliph rewarded Abu al-Atahiyah with the highest prize, declaring: 'The first flattered my vanity; the second diverted my leisure; but the third was my true friend, for he reminded my soul of its eternal accountability.'
moral: True poetry speaks truth to power, reminding rulers that justice and humility are their only enduring shields.
